reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: A group of lysosomal storage disorders caused by deficiency of specific enzymes needed to degrade glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides), leading to their accumulation in tissues and excretion in urine
Most subtypes are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner; the notable exception is MPS II (Hunter syndrome), which is X-linked recessive
Shared features across many subtypes include coarse facial features, short stature, joint stiffness or contractures, hepatosplenomegaly, and dysostosis multiplex on radiographs
Corneal clouding is prominent in several subtypes (for example MPS I and MPS VI) but characteristically absent in MPS II and in the neuronopathic MPS III
Neurocognitive decline is a major feature of severe MPS I, MPS II, and especially MPS III (Sanfilippo), whereas MPS IV (Morquio) primarily affects the skeleton with preserved intellect
Cardiac valve disease, airway narrowing, hearing loss, and carpal tunnel syndrome are common and progressive complications
Cervical spine instability and cord compression are important risks, particularly in Morquio syndrome
Enzyme replacement therapy exists for several subtypes, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can benefit selected patients, most notably severe MPS I when performed early
reference.pathophysiology: The mucopolysaccharidoses arise from deficiency of one of the lysosomal enzymes required for the stepwise degradation of glycosaminoglycans such as dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate. Incomplete breakdown leads to progressive accumulation of partially degraded glycosaminoglycans within lysosomes across many tissues, including connective tissue, cartilage, bone, cornea, heart valves, airways, and the central nervous system. This storage produces the progressive, multisystem, and often neurodegenerative phenotypes. The specific enzyme deficiency and the glycosaminoglycans that accumulate determine the clinical subtype.
additionalDifferentials: Other lysosomal storage disorders such as the oligosaccharidoses and mucolipidoses
GM1 gangliosidosis with coarse features and skeletal changes
additionalInvestigations: Urinary glycosaminoglycan quantification and electrophoresis as a screening step
Specific lysosomal enzyme assays to identify the subtype
Molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling
Skeletal survey to demonstrate dysostosis multiplex and assess spine stability
Echocardiography, audiology, ophthalmology, and airway assessment for multisystem involvement
redFlags: Signs of cervical spine instability or spinal cord compression
Progressive airway obstruction or obstructive sleep apnoea
Cardiac valve disease or heart failure
Rapid neurocognitive regression in neuronopathic subtypes
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely by subtype and severity. Severe neuronopathic forms progress to early disability and death, while attenuated forms are compatible with longer survival. Enzyme replacement and, for selected patients, stem cell transplantation can slow somatic disease, but established skeletal and neurological damage is often irreversible and does not fully respond to enzyme therapy.
pitfalls: Missing early disease because features can be subtle in infancy and evolve over time
Overlooking cervical spine risk before anaesthesia or intubation
Assuming enzyme replacement will reverse neurological or advanced skeletal disease
Not recognising the X-linked inheritance of MPS II when counselling families
management: Give enzyme replacement therapy for the subtypes where it exists, using laronidase for MPS I, idursulfase for MPS II, galsulfase for MPS VI and elosulfase alfa for MPS IVA, to slow somatic disease
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe MPS I (Hurler) in early infancy to preserve neurocognition
Manage the airway carefully, treating obstructive disease and anticipating a difficult airway and cervical instability during anaesthesia
Undertake cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and manage progressive valve disease
Provide orthopaedic and spinal surgery for dysostosis multiplex, cervical cord compression and carpal tunnel syndrome
Address hearing loss with aids, treat hydrocephalus with shunting and provide ophthalmological care for corneal clouding
Offer genetic counselling, noting most subtypes are autosomal recessive while MPS II (Hunter) is X-linked recessive
